notes.meaning: The believers gathered in one place in complete harmony on the Jewish feast of Pentecost, fifty days after Passover. Their old quarrels about who was greatest had ended, and they were praying together with one heart. God chose this special harvest festival to send His Holy Spirit upon them.

A loud roar suddenly sounded from heaven and filled the entire house where they were sitting. It sounded like a violent, rushing wind, though it was a supernatural sound rather than regular air. This sudden sign showed that the Spirit of God was arriving from heaven with great power.

The believers saw what looked like small flames of fire parting and coming to rest on each person. This fire was a visible picture of the Spirit purifying their hearts and touching their tongues for speech. It rested on every believer present, showing that each one was given grace and power to serve.

Every person in the room was filled with the Holy Spirit and began speaking in foreign languages they had never learned. The Spirit gave them the exact words to speak with boldness and clarity. This miracle equipped ordinary disciples to proclaim the good news to people of all nations.

differ.view: The visible, miraculous gifts like these have ceased, though the Spirit himself never leaves the church. Missionaries must now learn languages by careful study.
Believers today can still seek and receive the same filling of the Spirit, even more than once, for bold witness. They should not expect wind or flames.

notes.meaning: Devout Jewish worshipers from many different countries were staying in Jerusalem for the harvest feast. Some lived there permanently, while others had traveled long distances out of love for God and His law. God brought these sincere worshipers together at the exact right moment to hear His message.

When the sound of the believers speaking rang out, a large crowd rushed together in complete shock. Each foreign visitor was astonished to hear his own native language being spoken clearly. The people were deeply puzzled and could hardly believe what they were hearing.

The listeners were stunned because the speakers were all from Galilee, an area known for simple workers with rough local accents. The crowd could not fathom how these uneducated men could speak foreign languages so fluently. Yet every visitor clearly heard the disciples speaking the dialect of the land where he was born.

Luke lists fifteen regions spanning from Persia in the east to Rome in the west, representing the whole known world. Both Jews by birth and Gentile converts to Judaism heard these believers declaring the wonderful works of God in their own native tongues. This event gave a preview of how the message of Jesus would soon spread across every border.

The crowd remained completely amazed and thoroughly puzzled, asking one another what this great event meant. They recognized that a supernatural work was taking place right before their eyes, but they did not know its purpose. Their honest questioning prepared them to hear the explanation God was about to give.

Some onlookers began to make fun of the disciples, sneering that they were simply drunk on sweet, strong wine. When people do not want to accept God's power, they often resort to foolish insults and mockery. Their harsh comment showed closed minds toward a clear work of God.

Peter stepped forward with the other eleven apostles and addressed the large crowd with a loud, confident voice. Matthias stood beside him to show that the apostles were completely united in their witness. The same disciple who had once denied Jesus out of fear was now filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke with holy courage.

Peter quickly answered the mockers with plain common sense, pointing out that it was only nine o'clock in the morning. Jews did not eat or drink wine before the morning hour of prayer, especially during a holy festival. It was absurd to claim that a whole company of people was drunk so early in the day.

Peter told the crowd that this event was the fulfillment of what the prophet Joel had announced centuries before. The wonder they were witnessing was not caused by alcohol, but by God pouring out His Spirit as promised. Peter turned straight to the Scriptures to settle their confusion and point them to God's truth.

God promised that in the final age of salvation He would pour out His Spirit freely on all kinds of people. In the past, the Spirit rested mainly on a few chosen leaders, but now sons and daughters, young and old, and even slaves would receive Him. God shows no favoritism, giving His power to anyone who belongs to Him so they can speak His truth.

The prophecy describes terrifying signs in the sky and on the earth, like blood, fire, smoke, and a darkened sun and moon, before God's great day arrives. These strong images show the awful danger of facing God's judgment and the downfall of corrupt systems. God warns men through these portents so they will wake up and seek mercy before it is too late.

differ.view: Pentecost was only a near or partial fulfilment of Joel. The complete fulfilment of these signs is still ahead, in a time of great trouble at the end of the age.

notes.meaning: In the middle of warnings about coming judgment, God gives a glorious promise of rescue. Anyone at all who sincerely calls upon the Lord in faith will be delivered from guilt and eternal ruin. Salvation is freely offered to everyone who trusts in God's mercy.

Peter turned the focus of his message directly to Jesus of Nazareth, whom his listeners knew well. God publicly proved that Jesus was His chosen Messiah by performing miracles, wonders, and signs through Him right in their midst. The crowd could not deny these facts because they had seen them with their own eyes.

Jesus was handed over and nailed to a cross by pagan Roman hands, just as the crowd had demanded. Yet this terrible event was not an accident; it happened according to God's eternal plan and foreknowledge to redeem the world. Men were fully responsible and guilty for their wicked acts, even while God was using them to fulfill His saving purpose.

differ.view: God did not merely foresee what happened to Christ but decreed it. His providence (his rule over all things) governs everything, even evil acts, yet he is never the author of evil.
God decreed that his Son would be the sacrifice, out of love for the world. But he only allowed, and did not order, the wicked means of Judas's betrayal and the people's malice.

notes.meaning: God broke the power of the grave and raised Jesus back to life. Because Jesus was completely innocent and holy, it was impossible for death to keep its grip on Him. His resurrection proved beyond doubt that His sacrifice for sin was fully accepted by God the Father.
